overview.title: Tarot on the Tree of Life
overview.subtitle: An introduction
paragraphs: Explore the Tree of Life through its ten sephiroth and twenty-two connecting paths. Above Kether are Ain, Ain Soph and Ain Soph Aur: three ways of approaching what precedes manifestation.

The sephiroth relate to the numbered cards and court cards of tarot; the twenty-two connecting paths relate to the Hebrew letters and Major Arcana. Hover to explore an entry, or select it to keep its correspondences and longer notes open.

sections.title: A map for study
paragraphs: In A Garden of Pomegranates, Israel Regardie presents the Tree as a symbolic alphabet for arranging ideas and experience. Its thirty-two divisions bring together religious, philosophical and other forms of knowledge. The ten sephiroth and twenty-two connecting paths together form the thirty-two Paths of Wisdom.

His filing-cabinet analogy leaves room for personal study: a label provides a place to begin, while experience gradually gives its contents meaning. Learning the associations is one stage; comparing them, reflecting on them and seeing their relationships is the continuing work.

sections.title: How to read correspondences
paragraphs: A correspondence links things through a shared quality. It does not make those things identical. Regardie illustrates this with Geburah: Mars, the sword, tobacco and the basilisk can all express qualities associated with the number five without becoming interchangeable.

The entries follow the particular attributions in these pages. Their comparisons between deities, philosophies, colours, plants and tarot belong to the author’s Hermetic Qabalistic interpretation. Read each association in the aspect described: the same deity can appear at more than one place on the Tree for a different reason.

sections.title: Three triads and the Kingdom
paragraphs: Kether, Chokmah and Binah form the Supernal Triad. The book describes the Abyss beneath them as the metaphysical distinction between ideal principles and their expression in the seven lower sephiroth.

Chesed, Geburah and Tiphareth form the second triad; Netzach, Hod and Yesod form the third. Malkuth gathers the preceding nine into the world of matter and sense experience. Each sephirah has its own character, receives from above and passes on both what it receives and its particular nature.

sections.title: Tarot on the Tree
paragraphs: The numbered cards run from the four Aces at Kether to the four Tens at Malkuth. The court-card attributions in this edition are Kings at Chokmah, Queens at Binah, Princes or Knights (Jacks) at Tiphareth, and Princesses at Malkuth. These source terms are retained because court-card titles vary between decks.

For the connecting paths, each Hebrew letter has an alphabetic position, a numerical value, a position on the Tree, a tarot attribution and a meaning when its name is spelled out. The chapter treats these letters and numbers as a language of relationships whose significance develops through study.

The opening pages also recount a legend of wisdom being preserved in the seventy-eight pictures of tarot. Regardie explicitly says he cannot vouch for that story’s accuracy; it is presented here as part of the book’s symbolic account of tarot.

sections.title: Working with the map
paragraphs: The chapter proposes three related uses: analysing an idea through the Tree, finding connections between ideas, and translating one symbolic system into another. Its image of a living Tree suggests that understanding grows as the associations become familiar.

Names on this diagram use familiar spellings. Within each entry, source spellings such as Keser, Tipharas, Netsach and Malkus are recorded where they differ. Select Ain or either of the other veils to read the account of the limitless and the emergence of Kether.

source.title: Israel Regardie · A Garden of Pomegranates

parts.title: Kether
parts.subtitle: The Crown
paragraphs: Kether, the Crown, is the first sephirah and the source of the Tree’s unfolding. The book calls it Keser: the primordial, dimensionless point in which the other nine sephiroth are present in potential.
Its unity is described as a Monad, a centre of spiritual energy and consciousness. It begins the manifested order while receiving from what lies beyond that order: Ain, Ain Soph and Ain Soph Aur.

correspondences.label: Titles
correspondences.value: The Crown; the Monad; First Cause or Demiurgos; Macroprosopus, the Great Countenance

correspondences.label: Deities
correspondences.value: Ptah; Amon-Ra, with whom the text associates Osiris; Zeus / Jupiter; Brahma

sections.title: From the limitless to the point
paragraphs: The account begins with Ain, then Ain Soph as Infinity and Ain Soph Aur as Limitless Light. By the contraction called Tsimtsum, that light is described as concentrating into Kether. Another image presents primordial whirling forces heralding the first point from which manifestation proceeds.

The point is metaphysical: the author uses it to express an indivisible origin of life, activity and force. His comparison with Leibniz’s Monad gives it both the character of a root of things and a unit of consciousness.

sections.title: The source and the ten
paragraphs: In the Zohar’s water analogy, Kether is the source, Chokmah the issuing current and Binah the receiving sea. Seven channels extend from them, completing the ten. Regardie describes the sephiroth as principles or vessels of force through which universal consciousness expresses itself.

One remains the basis of number; ten completes the series and returns to units. Kether’s titles First Cause and Great Countenance express this originating role. Ahieh, translated here as “I will be,” stresses an active process of becoming rather than a finished, static creation.

sections.title: Creators and their emanations
paragraphs: Ptah is associated with the cosmic egg, Amon-Ra with divine kingship, and Zeus or Jupiter with the highest father and ruler. Brahma appears as creator; the seven Prajapati proceeding from him are compared with the seven lower sephiroth.

The chapter places these divine images within a philosophy of one consciousness differentiated into many powers. Its gods, angels and spirits represent different functions and degrees of that manifestation; names express particular powers and qualities.

sections.title: The character of the symbols
paragraphs: The diamond suggests permanence and brilliance. The swan signifies spirit, ecstasy and discriminating wisdom: the Hansa legend tells of separating milk from water. The hawk’s elevated, detached gaze expresses the Monad’s point of view.

Ambergris is compared with a foundation that draws out the qualities of other perfumes. White and the four Aces likewise give this entry the character of a beginning from which many expressions can develop.

sections.title: Receiving and transmitting
paragraphs: The chapter closes the Kether entry with a principle attributed to Rabbi Azariel: every sephirah has its own function, receives from what precedes it, and communicates both its own nature and the influence received to what follows. Kether receives from above the numbered Tree.

source.title: Israel Regardie · A Garden of Pomegranates

palette.name: White
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Chokmah
parts.subtitle: Wisdom
paragraphs: Chokmah is Wisdom, the second sephirah and the active, energizing expression of Kether’s unity. The chapter calls it the Father and pairs it with Binah, the Mother, in the Supernal Triad.

The book approaches the emergence of two through reflection: one becomes distinguishable from its image. Chokmah expresses the originating current of consciousness, before Binah gives that current a receiving form.

correspondences.label: Astrology
correspondences.value: Uranus in this text; the Zodiac (Mazlos) as the traditional attribution

correspondences.label: Tarot
correspondences.value: The four Twos; the four Kings

correspondences.label: Deities
correspondences.value: Tahuti / Thoth; Pallas Athena / Minerva; Maat; Uranus; Hermes; Kwan Shi Yin; Vishnu; Ishvara

correspondences.label: Related ideas
correspondences.value: Yang; Purusha; Mahat or Cosmic Ideation; the Word, Logos and Memrah

sections.title: Wisdom as an active principle
paragraphs: The Father and Mother language expresses the chapter’s symbolic polarity of activity and receptivity. Chokmah is the vigorous, initiating aspect. The author also uses a geometrical analogy: the point extends into a line, the line into a plane and the plane into a body.

Its names Word, Logos and Memrah indicate an ordering or expressing principle. The comparisons with Purusha and Cosmic Ideation concern the underlying spiritual reality of consciousness, rather than knowledge understood only as accumulated facts.

sections.title: Divine images of intelligence
paragraphs: Thoth contributes writing, learning and magic; his ibis and attendant baboon belong to that image. Athena or Minerva joins intellectual gifts with power and wisdom, while Maat supplies truth. Hermes represents transmission of the influence from Kether.
Uranus brings the image of the starry heavens. The book explicitly distinguishes its attribution of Uranus from the traditional Zodiac attribution, so both are retained here.

sections.title: Immortality, the star and the Father
paragraphs: Amaranth is interpreted as a flower of immortality. The star ruby expresses the creative star’s active energy, while turquoise recalls the Zodiac. Grey and musk complete the listed sensory correspondences.
Yod is the first letter of the divine name YHVH in the book’s scheme. Through this Father attribution, the four Kings accompany the four Twos. These court-card names follow this edition.

source.title: Israel Regardie · A Garden of Pomegranates

palette.name: Grey
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Binah
parts.subtitle: Understanding
paragraphs: Binah is Understanding, the third sephirah and Aimah, the Mother. It completes the Supernal Triad with Kether and Chokmah. Where Chokmah supplies the formative impulse, Binah is the receptive principle through which form becomes possible.
Its Great Sea image is the basin receiving the current in the chapter’s water analogy. The author extends this idea to the underlying substance of physical and mental phenomena alike.

correspondences.label: Titles
correspondences.value: Aimah, the Mother; the Great Sea

correspondences.label: Tarot
correspondences.value: The four Threes; the four Queens

correspondences.label: Symbol
correspondences.value: The brooding dove; Shechinah or Holy Spirit

correspondences.label: Deities
correspondences.value: Saturn / Kronos; Frigg; Shakti; Maya; Kwan Yin; Kali; Isis

sections.title: The Mother and the formation of things
paragraphs: Binah is described as receptive, feminine and passive within the book’s symbolic polarity. Its role is substantive: it provides the vehicle in which an idea or force can take shape. Chokmah is compared with the formative essence of consciousness, and Binah with the root substance underlying its expressions.

The author associates this with Shakti’s power to unite forms, Maya’s world of appearance, Yin and the Theosophical idea of Mulaprakriti. These comparisons belong to his attempt to read different traditions through a common set of qualities.

sections.title: Creation, destruction and time
paragraphs: Saturn and Kronos connect Binah with time; Frigg provides a maternal image. Kali expresses Nature’s simultaneous creating and destroying: the chapter describes both her terrible imagery of skulls and sword and her gestures of generosity and fearlessness. Isis supplies a corresponding beneficent aspect.

Black expresses receptivity in this account. The pearl links the sea with hidden growth in the oyster, while the brooding dove represents the divine presence that the text associates with the Supernal Mother.

sections.title: Above the Abyss
paragraphs: Kether, Chokmah and Binah are the three Supernals. The chapter describes them as ideal principles beyond ordinary intellectual conception. The Abyss names the metaphysical gap between these principles and the seven lower sephiroth that express them.

Regardie acknowledges a difficulty in explaining how an unknowable absolute can produce manifestation. The images of unity, duality and trinity, and of the Great Breath creating and withdrawing worlds, are ways of approaching that question. They do not remove the limits of an intellectual explanation.

sections.title: The first Heh and the Queens
paragraphs: Binah receives the first Heh of YHVH and the four Queens, alongside the four Threes. The later Daughter image at Malkuth reflects this Mother: the chapter presents the divine presence in the material world as an expression of Binah’s power.

source.title: Israel Regardie · A Garden of Pomegranates

palette.name: Black
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Chesed
parts.subtitle: Mercy
paragraphs: Chesed means Mercy and also bears the name Gedulah, Majesty or Greatness. As the fourth sephirah it begins the second triad, which reflects the Supernal Triad at a further stage of manifestation.
Its Jupiter attribution expresses greatness and beneficence. The text also gives it Water and a receptive character, bringing several qualities together within the same sephirah.

correspondences.label: Deities
correspondences.value: Poseidon; Jupiter / Zeus; Indra; Amoun; Thor; Æger

sections.title: Mercy and the second triad
paragraphs: Chesed, Geburah and Tiphareth form the second triad, with blue, red and yellow as their respective colours. Chesed and Geburah supply contrasting powers that are reconciled in Tiphareth.

The chapter calls the fourth through ninth sephiroth the Potencies of Construction. It relates them to the dimensions and directions through which manifestation is understood, with positive and negative poles belonging to the same structure.

sections.title: Water, thunder and greatness
paragraphs: Poseidon contributes dominion over the sea. Jupiter is considered in the early Roman aspect of rain, storms and thunder; Zeus and Indra supply related thunderbolt imagery. The book also attributes Amoun, Thor and the sea god Æger to this group.
The author includes Æger’s skill in magic in the comparison and associates Jupiter with the working of the Tetragrammaton. These are different facets of the quality represented by Chesed.

sections.title: Receptivity and balance
paragraphs: Chesed stands in the right-hand Pillar of Mercy and is described as active or masculine in the arrangement of the Tree. Its water imagery and Receptacular Intelligence title also stress receptivity. The chapter treats such overlapping qualities as part of balance within the system.

The horse is connected through the story of Poseidon’s creation of it and the teaching of horsemanship. The unicorn accompanies it. Blue, tin, cedar, the amethyst and sapphire, and the pine, olive and shamrock complete the correspondences listed on these pages.

source.title: Israel Regardie · A Garden of Pomegranates

palette.name: Blue
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Geburah
parts.subtitle: Strength
paragraphs: Geburah is Strength or Power, the fifth sephirah. The chapter presents it as arising from Chesed while reflecting Binah at a lower level. Its martial character gives force and severity a place beside mercy.
Chesed and Geburah are described together through expansion and contraction. Their opposing powers contribute to the equilibrium expressed by Tiphareth.

correspondences.label: Deities
correspondences.value: Mars; Ares; Thor; Nephthys as the Lady of Severity

sections.title: Strength and severity
paragraphs: Mars and Ares express the character of conflict and power. Thor supplies strength, armour, the fiery gaze and the battle chariot. Nephthys, described here as the shadowy counterpart of Isis and Lady of Severity, connects this entry with Binah.

The sword, spear, scourge and burin are grouped as instruments that express concentrated force. Iron and oak reinforce strength; the fiery or stinging character of tobacco and nettle provides the author’s reason for their inclusion.

sections.title: The Pillar of Severity
paragraphs: Geburah occupies the left-hand Pillar of Severity, assigned a feminine polarity in the chapter’s arrangement. Many of its individual correspondences are nevertheless masculine or martial. The text uses this mixture, and the receptive qualities found in Chesed, to emphasize equilibrium within each side.

The paired fourth and fifth sephiroth are compared with expansive and contracting, centripetal and centrifugal energies operating under the Logos associated with Chokmah. Their relationship matters as much as either list of symbols considered alone.

sections.title: Red, the ruby and the basilisk
paragraphs: The bright scarlet ruby agrees with Geburah’s red colour. The basilisk contributes the legendary power of the fixed or destructive gaze. The four Fives and the title Radical Intelligence complete the entry’s principal correspondences.

The chapter later uses Geburah to explain the method: Mars, a plant, a creature and a weapon may correspond through a shared quality of force. That relationship does not make one literally equivalent to another.

source.title: Israel Regardie · A Garden of Pomegranates

palette.name: Red
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Tiphareth
parts.subtitle: Beauty and Harmony
paragraphs: Tiphareth is Beauty and Harmony, the sixth sephirah at the centre of the Tree. The chapter describes it as the reconciliation of Chesed and Geburah, completing the second triad.

Its Sun attribution expresses a central source of life and light. The text develops that image into spiritual consciousness, balance and an ethical ideal in which spirit and matter are brought into equilibrium.

correspondences.label: Tarot
correspondences.value: The four Sixes; the four Princes or Knights (Jacks), in the book’s terminology

correspondences.label: Deities
correspondences.value: Ra; Apollo; Hari / Krishna; Adonis; Iacchus; Rama; Asar; Dionysius / Bacchus; Balder, suggested by the author

correspondences.label: Related figure
correspondences.value: Microprosopus, the Lesser Countenance: the grouping of sephiroth around Tiphareth

sections.title: The central Sun
paragraphs: The reconciliation of the fourth and fifth sephiroth places Tiphareth at the centre of the diagram, like a Sun around which the other planetary attributions are arranged. Its yellow colour and yellow jewels repeat this solar imagery.

Ra appears as a hawk-headed deity or winged solar disk. Apollo represents inward or intellectual illumination, fair reason and harmony. Hari, identified with Krishna, supplies the image of a divine incarnation in which spiritual and material life are balanced.

sections.title: Beauty, inspiration and renewal
paragraphs: Adonis, Iacchus, Rama and Asar are attributed through beauty or solar symbolism. Dionysius brings youth, beauty, the vine and the image of mystical inspiration. Under the name Bacchus, he represents the possibility of spiritual renewal and union with the divine.

The chapter suggests Balder as a Norse correspondence because of his beauty and goodness. Its Lesser Countenance title applies to the sephiroth grouped around Tiphareth, expressing an ordered whole centred on this principle of harmony.

sections.title: The lion and the life-giving birds
paragraphs: The lion carries kingship, creative solar force and the story of Dionysius taking a lion’s form. The chapter also relates the lion image to Leo and the midsummer Sun.

The phoenix and pelican are presented through legends of a parent giving its life or blood to nourish its young. The interpretation is redemptive self-giving. The story of Semele, Zeus and the second birth of Dionysius provides a further image of life renewed through sacrifice.

sections.title: Resurrection, the Son and tarot
paragraphs: Acacia is associated with resurrection in Masonic symbolism; the vine continues the Dionysian theme. Olibanum is the perfume, and topaz and yellow diamond belong through their colour.

The four Sixes correspond to this sixth sephirah. The Son attribution joins Vav, the third letter of YHVH, to the four Princes or Knights (Jacks). Keeping the book’s full court-card wording makes the correspondence usable with its particular naming system.

source.title: Israel Regardie · A Garden of Pomegranates

palette.name: Yellow
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.tarotNote: The book’s Princes or Knights (Jacks) are shown here with the Rider–Waite Knights.

parts.title: Netzach
parts.subtitle: Victory
paragraphs: Netzach is Victory, also called Eternity and Triumph in these pages. It is the seventh sephirah and the first of the third triad, followed by Hod and Yesod.

Its Venus attribution brings together love, beauty, attraction and the generative life of Nature. The chapter extends victory from the triumph of light into images of flourishing, fertility and the harvest.

sections.title: Victory and the morning
paragraphs: The chapter introduces Nike through Walter Pater’s account of victory as the triumph of morning over darkness. The goddess guiding a hero’s chariot or crowning a victor retains something of this bright, life-giving image.
Netzach therefore carries more than victory in conflict. Its associations gather the beauty, vitality and attraction through which life succeeds and continues.

sections.title: Love and the fruits of the earth
paragraphs: Aphrodite or Venus supplies love and beauty, especially the power of attraction and sexual love. Hathor, described as a lesser aspect of Isis, appears as a cow goddess of generative Nature, agriculture and the earth’s fruits. Bhavani is the Hindu correspondence named here.
The rose belongs through its affinity with Aphrodite. Red sandalwood and benzoin contribute the sensuous character that the author associates with Venus.

sections.title: The third triad
paragraphs: Netzach’s green is explained as a union of Chesed’s blue and Tiphareth’s yellow. Its place in the Tree thus continues the relationships established in the preceding triad.

Netzach and Hod together lead to Yesod. In the discussion of their pairing, Victory and Splendour are associated with extension, multiplication and force: the continued expression of the powers that unfold through the Tree. The four Sevens give Netzach its numbered tarot correspondence.

source.title: Israel Regardie · A Garden of Pomegranates

palette.name: Green
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Hod
parts.subtitle: Splendour
paragraphs: Hod is Splendour, the eighth sephirah, standing opposite Netzach in the third triad. Mercury gives its correspondences the character of intelligence, invention, communication and mediation.
The chapter describes Hod as expressing qualities similar to Chokmah at a lower level of the Tree. Together, Netzach and Hod contribute the forces gathered into Yesod.

correspondences.label: Other botanical attribution
correspondences.value: Anhalonium Lewinii — the historical name used in the text

correspondences.label: Animal images
correspondences.value: Jackal, through Anubis; ape or monkey, through Hanuman

sections.title: Mercury and the arts of intelligence
paragraphs: Hermes supplies prudence, shrewdness, resourcefulness and invention. The chapter associates him with the alphabet, mathematics, astronomy, weights and measures, commerce and good fortune. His role as messenger expresses movement and communication between different orders of experience.

His guidance of the dead into the lower world is compared with Anubis leading the soul towards the judgment of Osiris. This is one particular connection between their functions within the author’s comparative system.

sections.title: Mind and its images
paragraphs: Hanuman provides the Hindu correspondence. The author relates the ape or monkey image to a Theosophical account of the Manasaputras, the mind-born sons of Brahma, to explain an association with mind and intelligence.

Moly and the botanical name Anhalonium Lewinii appear among the attributions. The latter is discussed in the source in connection with visionary colour and introspection. They are included here as the chapter’s correspondences.

sections.title: Splendour in the third triad
paragraphs: Orange combines Geburah’s red with Tiphareth’s yellow, just as Netzach’s green combines blue and yellow. The opal, storax and four Eights complete Hod’s principal sensory and tarot associations.
The author reads Victory and Splendour together as extension, multiplication and force. Their relationship leads into Yesod’s stable foundation, where the influences expressed above are gathered.

source.title: Israel Regardie · A Garden of Pomegranates

palette.name: Orange
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Yesod
parts.subtitle: Foundation
paragraphs: Yesod is Foundation, the ninth sephirah. It results from the relationship of Netzach and Hod and completes the third triad.

The chapter describes it as the subtle basis upon which the physical world is formed. Its lunar character is receptive and reflective: influences from above are gathered here as the Moon receives the Sun’s light.

correspondences.label: Related ideas
correspondences.value: The Astral Plane; Astral Light; Anima Mundi, the Soul of the World

correspondences.label: Animal images
correspondences.value: Elephant and tortoise, through the image of Ganesha

sections.title: Change with stability
paragraphs: The source’s central phrase for Yesod is change with stability. It imagines the continuous ebb and flow of forces as the foundation that sustains the world. The Astral Light is described within this occult account as a subtle medium providing the pattern for physical forms.

Yesod gathers potentialities and reproductive power. The Zohar passage cited by the author places seed, energy and the return of things to their foundation here. This gives Foundation both a supporting and a generative meaning.

sections.title: Support, reflection and the Moon
paragraphs: Shu is shown lifting Nuit, the heavens, from the body of Seb, the earth. Ganesha removes obstacles and supports the universe while standing upon a tortoise in the image given by the text. Diana contributes the lunar attribution.
The book also records an occult image of the Moon as a dead yet living body containing active and destructive powers. That description belongs to its magical symbolism of lunar influence.

sections.title: The Soul of the World
paragraphs: Some writers cited in the chapter call the Astral Light Anima Mundi, the Soul of the World. Regardie compares this with Jung’s collective unconscious. The comparison is his interpretation of a shared underlying field of life and consciousness.
Mandrake, damiana and jasmine are grouped through the source’s reproductive and sensual associations. Purple, the four Nines and Pure or Clear Intelligence complete the entry.

source.title: Israel Regardie · A Garden of Pomegranates

palette.name: Purple
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Malkuth
parts.subtitle: The Kingdom
paragraphs: Malkuth is the Kingdom, the tenth sephirah. It gathers the preceding nine into the world of the four elements: matter and the forms perceived through the five senses.
Below the three triads, Malkuth gives their ideas a concrete expression. The chapter also places the divine presence within this material world, connecting the Kingdom with both Binah and Kether.

correspondences.label: Titles
correspondences.value: The Kingdom; the Virgin; the Bride; the Daughter

correspondences.label: Domain
correspondences.value: The physical world; the four elements; the five senses

correspondences.label: Tarot
correspondences.value: The four Tens; the four Princesses

correspondences.label: Deities and figures
correspondences.value: Seb, as named in the text; Psyche; the lower Nephthys; the unmarried Isis; Persephone; Ceres; Lakshmi; the Sphinx

correspondences.label: Divine presence
correspondences.value: Shechinah, described here as the Daughter or expression of Binah

sections.title: The Kingdom and the embodied world
paragraphs: Malkuth synthesizes the whole numerical sequence. The book describes the previous nine ideas as crystallizing into the forms of the sensory world. The four elements and five senses make this the place of embodied experience.

Its earth and fertility images include Persephone, Ceres, Lakshmi and the Sphinx. Psyche, Nephthys and Isis provide further images of the soul or receptive life. The source names Seb and connects its Egyptian imagery with gross matter.

sections.title: The presence within matter
paragraphs: The chapter describes Shechinah as the spiritual presence of Ain Soph abiding in the world where souls are embodied. This is its explanation of the relationship between the highest and lowest: Kether is in Malkuth and Malkuth in Kether, each in a different manner.

It distinguishes Binah as the Supernal Mother from the presence expressed in Malkuth as her image or Daughter. In the interpretation quoted from Isaac Myer, this is the executive power of the Upper Mother acting within manifestation.

sections.title: The final Heh and the Princesses
paragraphs: The final Heh of YHVH and the four Princesses continue the Daughter attribution. Malkuth also receives the four Tens, completing the numbered tarot sequence that begins with Kether’s Aces.

Its four colours are citrine, olive, russet and black. Dittany of Crete is attributed through the dense clouds produced by its incense, an image of substantial manifestation. Its Yetsiratic title is Resplendent Intelligence.

source.title: Israel Regardie · A Garden of Pomegranates

palette.name: Citrine; olive; russet; black
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.tarotNote: The book’s Princesses are shown here with the Rider–Waite Pages.

parts.title: Aleph
parts.subtitle: Kether — Chokmah
paragraphs: Aleph is the first Hebrew letter, associated here with the ox or bull and the generative power of nature. The text relates it to breath, air and the beginning of creative movement.

correspondences.label: Deities / figures
correspondences.value: Hoor-paar-Kraat; Zeus and Jupiter; the Maruts (Vayu); the Valkyries

correspondences.label: Symbols
correspondences.value: Ox-yoke; Thor’s thunderbolt; the ancient swastika as a symbol of primordial motion in the text

sections.title: The Fool
paragraphs: The card is described as a jester carrying a bundle on a stick, with a precipice ahead and a small dog behind. A pentagram on the tunic represents Spirit. The imagery is linked to air and unbounded movement.

palette.name: Sky blue
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Beth
parts.subtitle: Kether — Binah
paragraphs: Beth, pronounced “Bes” in these pages, is the second Hebrew letter and means house. Its symbolism connects inward activity, wisdom and language with Mercury.

correspondences.label: Practices mentioned
correspondences.value: Dharana; Pranayama; balancing on one leg in the Ibis posture

sections.title: The Magician
paragraphs: The card is described with a sword, cup, pantacle and sceptre on a table. One hand raises a wand while the other points down, linking above and below. The infinity sign above the head reinforces the card’s association with wisdom and magic.

sections.title: Further associations
paragraphs: The text connects Mercury with a fluid, changeable alchemical principle. Odin is associated with arranging the world, knowledge, poetry and the Norse runes. The caduceus is related to kundalini in the yoga practices mentioned.
A pronunciation note explains that the Hebrew dagesh changes certain consonant sounds: in the example given, B becomes V when the dot is omitted.

palette.name: Orange
palette.basis: Mercury, using the orange assigned to Hod in the supplied chapter; no separate colour is stated in the Beth entry.
palette.note: Orange follows Mercury’s association with Hod; the supplied Beth entry gives no separate colour.

parts.title: Gimel
parts.subtitle: Kether — Tiphareth
paragraphs: Gimel means camel. This lunar path joins Kether to Tiphareth across the Abyss, linking the Supernal Triad with the centre of the tree. The book compares that passage to a camel crossing a desert.

correspondences.label: Tarot
correspondences.value: II — The High Priestess of the Silver Star

sections.title: The High Priestess
paragraphs: The enthroned priestess wears a tiara and bears solar and lunar signs. She sits between a white pillar and a black pillar, compared with the two sides of the tree and the pillars Yachin and Boaz. Her scroll represents the Law. The book associates her with the Shechinah and, in another symbolic system, Babalon.

sections.title: The Silver Star
paragraphs: The Supernal Triad is identified with the Inner College of Masters in the Rosicrucian grade system described here. Gimel provides its connection to Tiphareth, making the lunar priestess an image of entry into that inner order.
The book gives G as the letter’s sound and describes a softer J sound when its dot is omitted.

palette.name: Silver
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Daleth
parts.subtitle: Chokmah — Binah
paragraphs: Daleth means door and is pronounced “Dallas” in these pages. Joining Chokmah and Binah, it connects the Father and Mother within the Supernal Triad. Venus expresses the attraction and union associated with this path.

correspondences.label: Deities / figures
correspondences.value: Aphrodite; Lalita, an aspect of Shakti; Hathor; Freya

sections.title: The Empress
paragraphs: The Empress holds a sceptre formed from a globe and cross. Venus appears on her robe and heart-shaped shield. Corn before her throne links love with agriculture and fertility; a green garland and pearl necklace complete the description.

sections.title: Union and fertility
paragraphs: The door is also interpreted as a symbol of the womb. Aphrodite’s girdle represents attraction and desire. In discussing these deities, the author treats them as expressions of natural forces rather than only as separate personalities.
The book describes Daleth as a double letter and compares its sound without the dot to the voiced th in “the” or “lather.”

palette.name: Green; emerald green
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: He
parts.subtitle: Chokmah — Tiphareth
paragraphs: He, written “Héh” in the text, means window. Its attribution is Aries, the ram: a sign ruled by Mars and in which the Sun is exalted. The book develops this path through images of courage, energy and will.

correspondences.label: Deities / figures
correspondences.value: Athena; Minerva; Shiva; Mars; Mentu; Tyr

correspondences.label: Related symbols
correspondences.value: Alchemical sulphur; Rajas, the quality of energy and volition

sections.title: The Emperor
paragraphs: The Emperor wears red and a ruby-set crown, seated on a throne carved with ram heads. His crossed legs and the triangle formed by his head and arms are read as the alchemical sign of sulphur, an image of active energy.

sections.title: Courage and protection
paragraphs: The martial figures are associated with protection, prudence, perseverance and honour in conflict. Athena and Minerva appear as protectors and guides; the hawk-headed Mentu and the Norse Tyr reinforce the connection with martial strength.

palette.name: Red
palette.basis: The Emperor’s red robe, described in the supplied He entry.
palette.note: Red follows the Emperor’s robe described in the supplied He entry.

parts.title: Vav
parts.subtitle: Chokmah — Chesed
paragraphs: Vav means nail and is attributed to Taurus, the bull. The book interprets the bull and the phallic symbolism of the letter as images of universal creative power and magical will.

correspondences.label: Symbols
correspondences.value: Bull; lingam; the Son of the Tetragrammaton

correspondences.label: Deities / figures
correspondences.value: Asar Ameshet; Apis; Shiva; Héré (Hera); Hymen; Bacchus / Dionysus-Zagreus; Adonis; Tammuz; Mithras; Attis

sections.title: The Hierophant
paragraphs: The Hierophant raises his right hand in blessing over two ministers and carries a staff surmounted by a cross. Two keys at his feet represent the mysteries of life and death.

sections.title: Creative power and redemption
paragraphs: The text connects the sacred bull with Shiva and the lingam, and discusses sacrificial bull imagery in the cult of Dionysus. Vav is also understood as the Son in the Tetragrammaton, relating this path to themes of redemption and to the figures associated with Tiphareth.
A pronunciation note gives V, U or O according to the position of the dot used with the letter.

palette.name: Indigo
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Zayin
parts.subtitle: Binah — Tiphareth
paragraphs: Zayin means sword; the letter’s shape is compared with a hilt and blade. Gemini, the twins, gives this path its emphasis on paired figures and complementary aspects.

correspondences.label: Deities / figures
correspondences.value: Rekht and Merti; Castor and Pollux; Apollo as diviner; Janus; Hoo-paar-Kraat

sections.title: The Lovers
paragraphs: The book contrasts older cards showing a man between two women, interpreted as Vice and Virtue or Lilith and Eve, with later cards showing a nude couple beneath an angel or Cupid with open wings.

sections.title: Paired aspects
paragraphs: Janus looks in two directions. Hoo-paar-Kraat is presented as combining Horus, associated with strength, and Harpocrates, associated with silence. Apollo’s connection here is specifically to divination, prophecy, dreams and healing.

palette.name: Mauve
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Cheth
parts.subtitle: Binah — Geburah
paragraphs: Cheth, pronounced “Ches” in the book with a guttural ch, means fence. It is assigned Cancer, described in the text as the celestial house of the soul. Its chariot imagery concerns the integration and direction of opposing forces.

correspondences.label: Deities / figures
correspondences.value: Khephra; Mercury as messenger; Apollo as charioteer; Hermod; Krishna as Arjuna’s charioteer

sections.title: The Chariot
paragraphs: An armoured figure rides beneath a blue canopy covered with stars. A silver star shines on the forehead, and crescent moons rest on the shoulders. A white sphinx and a black sphinx represent conflicting forces brought under direction. The chariot also bears a lingam and winged globe.

sections.title: The Great Work
paragraphs: The author reads the card as an image of the Great Work: integration of the self and attainment of the Knowledge and Conversation of the Holy Guardian Angel. The sphinx combines human and animal qualities as a symbol of that completed work. A related discussion treats libido as a broader energy of life, encompassing physiological and spiritual activity as well as sexuality.

palette.name: Maroon
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Teth
parts.subtitle: Chesed — Geburah
paragraphs: Teth, called “Tes” in the book, means serpent and is assigned Leo. This is the second horizontal or reciprocal path, joining Chesed with Geburah: mercy with might, and love with justice.

correspondences.label: Deities / figures
correspondences.value: Pasht; Sekket; Mau; Ra-Hoor-Khuit; Demeter; Venus as an agricultural goddess

sections.title: Strength
paragraphs: A woman crowned and girdled with flowers calmly closes a lion’s jaws. The scene presents strength exercised with composure and apparent ease.

sections.title: Lion and serpent
paragraphs: The lion ties the path to Leo and its solar ruler. The serpent and lion also carry alchemical and generative associations; the author discusses the serpent as a symbol of wisdom as well as sexuality.

palette.name: Purple
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Yod
parts.subtitle: Chesed — Tiphareth
paragraphs: Yod means hand, more specifically a hand with its index finger extended. The text interprets it as an image of creative will and the movement from potential into activity. Its zodiacal attribution is Virgo.

correspondences.label: Magical implements / symbols
correspondences.value: Wand; lamp; Eucharistic Host; the Hand of God

correspondences.label: Deities / figures
correspondences.value: Isis and Nephthys as unmarried figures; the Gopi; Narcissus; Adonis; Balder

sections.title: The Hermit
paragraphs: The card shows an aged adept, hooded and dressed in black, carrying a lamp in the right hand and a staff or wand in the left.

sections.title: Creative will and innocence
paragraphs: The pointed finger and wand are given phallic meanings, associated with the hidden will and the beginning of a new undertaking. Alongside this, Virgo’s correspondences emphasise innocence and purity through virgin figures, the snowdrop and narcissus, and Balder’s unpolluted dwelling.

palette.name: Grey
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Kaph
parts.subtitle: Chesed — Netzach
paragraphs: Kaph, pronounced “Caph” here, means spoon or the hollow of the hand. The receptive shape is linked with Jupiter’s generosity and abundance. The path joins Chesed, associated with Jupiter, to Netzach, associated with Venus.

correspondences.label: Deities / figures
correspondences.value: Jupiter; Zeus; Brahma; Indra; Pluto as giver of wealth; Njord

sections.title: The Wheel of Fortune
paragraphs: The wheel is described with Anubis, a demon carrying a trident, and a sword-bearing sphinx above. TARO and the four letters of the Tetragrammaton appear around it; the creatures of Ezekiel’s vision occupy the card’s corners.
The author reads the turning wheel as the cycle of karma and repeated existence, alternately raising and lowering worldly fortunes.

sections.title: Abundance and pronunciation
paragraphs: Pluto appears as a source of wealth, while Njord is linked with winds, the sea and possessions. The book gives a guttural ch sound when the letter’s dot is omitted, and a separate final form valued at 500.

palette.name: Blue
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Lamed
parts.subtitle: Geburah — Tiphareth
paragraphs: Lamed means ox-goad or whip. Its attribution to Libra, the scales, centres the path on balance, law and judgment. It joins Geburah with Tiphareth.

correspondences.label: Tarot titles
correspondences.value: The Daughter of the Lords of Truth; The Ruler of the Balances

sections.title: Justice
paragraphs: A solemn woman sits between two pillars with a sword in one hand and scales in the other. The card’s imagery mirrors Libra’s balance and the path’s concern with judgment.

sections.title: Law and judgment
paragraphs: Themis represents law and custom; Maat is connected with the weighing of the heart in the Egyptian judgment of the dead. Nemesis and Yama extend the comparison to consequences, death and the settling of deeds.

palette.name: Blue
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Mem
parts.subtitle: Geburah — Hod
paragraphs: Mem means water and is assigned the element of Water. Its shape is compared with waves. The path’s symbolism brings together the sea, sacramental drink and the figure of a saviour descending to bring light.

sections.title: The Hanged Man
paragraphs: A man in a blue tunic hangs by one foot from a T-shaped gibbet, his head surrounded by a golden halo. The bent leg forms a cross and his arms form a downward-pointing triangle. The author reads the inverted figure as a saviour bringing light to the earthly world.

sections.title: Water and sacrament
paragraphs: The cup and sacramental wine are connected with Soma, described as an elixir of immortality. The eagle, snake and scorpion are treated as kerubic symbols of Water, related respectively to humanity before redemption, magical force and final salvation.

palette.name: Sea green
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Nun
parts.subtitle: Tiphareth — Netzach
paragraphs: Nun, pronounced “Noon” in the text, means fish. Its sign is Scorpio, ruled here by Mars. The central theme is regeneration through decay: the transformation of an old condition into a new one.

sections.title: Death
paragraphs: The card is described as a black skeleton on a white horse carrying a scythe, recalling one of the Four Horsemen. It continues the path’s theme of dissolution as part of transformation.

sections.title: Regeneration
paragraphs: The alchemical comparison describes base matter passing through corruption or chemical change before yielding gold. The author also applies this pattern to the mystical dark night of the soul: a period of spiritual dryness understood as a preparation for renewal.
Khephra, the beetle associated here with the midnight Sun, represents light within darkness. Kundalini is described through the image of a coiled serpent at the base of the spine.

palette.name: Beetle-brown
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Samekh
parts.subtitle: Tiphareth — Yesod
paragraphs: Samekh, written “Samech” in the book, means prop. It is assigned Sagittarius and the upward-pointing arrow, which the author interprets as aspiration. The path rises from Yesod to Tiphareth, associated with the Sun.

correspondences.label: Deities / figures
correspondences.value: Diana; Apollo and Artemis as hunters; Ares

sections.title: Temperance
paragraphs: An angel in white robes bears a solar sign on the forehead. On the breast, the Tetragrammaton accompanies a gold triangle within a white square. Blue liquid passes from one golden chalice into another.

sections.title: Aspiration
paragraphs: The angel is interpreted as the Holy Guardian Angel toward whom the aspirant turns. The arrow, solar signs and triangle reinforce the movement from Yesod toward Tiphareth and the ideal of perfected humanity expressed by Asar-Un-Nefer.
The text also links jacinth with the myth of Hyacinth and Apollo.

palette.name: Green
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Ayin
parts.subtitle: Tiphareth — Hod
paragraphs: Ayin means eye, connected in the text with the eye of Shiva. Capricorn, the mountain goat, supplies the image of fearless upward movement. Its generative symbolism is interpreted as an expression of spiritual creative power.

correspondences.label: Letter / value
correspondences.value: ע · O (nasal, in the book’s notation) · 70

sections.title: The Devil
paragraphs: The figure is a winged, goat-headed satyr with a pentagram on the brow. One hand points upward while the other holds a downward-pointing flaming brand. A horned male and female figure are chained to the throne.

sections.title: Creative force
paragraphs: The author relates the yoni and lingam, the goat and the fertility deities to nature’s reproductive power. Bacchus and hemp add associations of intoxication and ecstasy. In the book’s spiritual interpretation, this force becomes conscious of its True Will and takes on a redemptive purpose.
The goat and ass are also connected with stories of Dionysus and Jesus riding an ass. Ayin is given a slightly nasal pronunciation.

palette.name: Black
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Peh
parts.subtitle: Netzach — Hod
paragraphs: Peh means mouth. Its shape is compared with Kaph’s hollow hand containing a small tongue or Yod. This is the third reciprocal path, joining Netzach and Hod, with Mars providing its martial correspondences.

correspondences.label: Deities / figures
correspondences.value: Horus; Mentu; Ares; Mars; Krishna as charioteer; Odin; the Valkyries

correspondences.label: Tarot titles
correspondences.value: The House of God; The Lord of the Hosts of the Mighty

sections.title: The Tower
paragraphs: Lightning strikes the crown-like top of a tower and breaks it apart. Flames emerge from three windows and two figures fall or leap from the structure. The card is also called the House of God.

sections.title: Martial force
paragraphs: Mars repeats many of Geburah’s associations on a different level of the tree. Warrior deities, iron, red stones and pungent scents develop that relationship. Odin and the Valkyries are included through their connection with battle and the fallen.
The book connects Peh and Kaph with a magical formula of the Adeptus Major grade. Without its dot, Peh is pronounced ph or f; its final form has the value 800.

palette.name: Red
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Tzaddi
parts.subtitle: Netzach — Yesod
paragraphs: Tzaddi, written “Tsaddi” in the book, means fish hook and is assigned Aquarius, the water-bearer. The path links Netzach’s Venus with Yesod’s Moon, which the author treats as two feminine influences.

correspondences.label: Tarot titles
correspondences.value: The Daughter of the Firmament; The Dweller between the Waters

sections.title: The Star
paragraphs: A nude woman kneels beside water, pouring from a jug in each hand. Seven eight-pointed stars surround a larger star above her, continuing the water-bearer imagery of Aquarius.

sections.title: Arts and the water-bearer
paragraphs: Juno represents womanhood in the book’s account, while Athena contributes associations with useful and elegant arts and the olive tree. Ganymede appears as cup-bearer, with the eagle recalling his ascent to Olympus. Chalcedony’s appearance is compared with watery clouds and stars.

palette.name: Sky blue
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Qoph
parts.subtitle: Netzach — Malkuth
paragraphs: Qoph means back of the head and is assigned Pisces, the fishes. The book relates this path to an aspect of the astral plane, using fish, water and the cloudy brilliance of pearl as its central images.

correspondences.label: Deities / figures
correspondences.value: Vishnu as the fish avatara; Neptune; Poseidon; Khephra; Jesus in Piscean symbolism; Oannes

sections.title: The Moon
paragraphs: Moonlight falls across a night landscape. A jackal and wolf howl between two towers while a crayfish or crab emerges from water onto dry land.

sections.title: Fish and the astral plane
paragraphs: The fish is treated as a generative symbol and compared across Vishnu’s fish incarnation, the Christian Ichthus and the fish-form of Oannes. The watery realm also supplies the links with Neptune and Poseidon.
Pearl’s cloudy lustre is compared with the forms and partly opaque visions of the astral plane, distinguished in the text from formless spiritual light.

palette.name: Buff
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Resh
parts.subtitle: Hod — Yesod
paragraphs: Resh means head and is attributed to the Sun. The book develops a consistent group of solar correspondences: gold, yellow, sun-loving plants and deities of the solar disk.

correspondences.label: Deities / figures
correspondences.value: Ra; Helios; Apollo; Surya; Horus; Kalki

sections.title: The Sun
paragraphs: A brilliant sun shines above a crowned child on a white horse, with sunflowers behind. The author identifies the child with Horus and connects the horse with Kalki.

sections.title: Pronunciation
paragraphs: Although the Sepher Yetsirah classifies Resh as a double letter, the author notes that he knows only its r sound. He tentatively suggests a strongly rolled r as a possible distinction.

palette.name: Yellow
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

parts.title: Shin
parts.subtitle: Hod — Malkuth
paragraphs: Shin means tooth, compared in the book with a three-pronged molar. Its element is Fire. The sound sh and the imagery of flame connect the letter with the descent of spirit.

correspondences.label: Deities / figures
correspondences.value: Agni; Hades; Vulcan; Pluto; Thoum-aesh-neith; Kabeshunt; Tarpesheth

correspondences.label: Spiritual imagery
correspondences.value: The Holy Spirit at Pentecost; Gabriel

sections.title: The Last Judgment
paragraphs: Gabriel sounds a trumpet bearing a banner with a red cross. The dead rise from opened tombs, looking upward and lifting their arms toward the angel.

sections.title: Fire and spirit
paragraphs: The author compares this path with the Holy Spirit descending as tongues of fire at Pentecost. Agni and the other fiery deities, fire opal and burning scents extend the elemental association.
The book distinguishes the sh sound of Shin from the s sound of Sin according to the dot’s position.

palette.name: Red
palette.basis: The Fire attribution of Shin; rendered red where the supplied entry gives no separate colour.
palette.note: Red represents Shin’s Fire attribution; the supplied entry gives no separate colour.

parts.title: Tav
parts.subtitle: Yesod — Malkuth
paragraphs: Tav means a T-shaped cross and joins Yesod to Malkuth. The book gives this path two related perspectives: the densest region of the astral plane, attributed to Saturn, and the universe considered as a whole.

correspondences.label: Deities / figures
correspondences.value: Brahma; Pan; Gaea or Ge; Vidar; Saturn; Sebek

correspondences.label: Card symbols
correspondences.value: The Virgin of the World; man, eagle, bull and lion

sections.title: The World
paragraphs: A female figure stands within a flowering wreath. The man, eagle, bull and lion occupy the four corners. The figure is described as the Virgin of the World, connected with Malkuth as the Daughter and the reflection below of the Shechinah above.

sections.title: Matter and the whole
paragraphs: Brahma, Pan, Gaea and Vidar express the totality and enduring substance of nature. Saturn is also associated with the earth and agriculture. In the denser interpretation, Sebek, strong unpleasant odours and the quality of inertia represent the grossest condition of matter.
The text gives an s pronunciation for Tav when its dot is absent.

palette.name: Black
palette.basis: Colour correspondence in the supplied book.

veils.title: Ain
veils.subtitle: Nothing · No-Thing
paragraphs: Ain is Nothing, or No-Thing: the unknowable origin before any shape, form or distinction. The chapter places it under the heading zero, before Kether and the ten sephiroth.
Regardie describes this as Infinite Space and a causeless source of manifestation. Ordinary names and definitions depend on limits; Ain is approached as that which precedes such limits.

source.title: Israel Regardie · A Garden of Pomegranates

correspondences.label: Position
correspondences.value: Before the ten sephiroth; zero in the chapter’s account

correspondences.label: Related names
correspondences.value: Infinite Space; the Absolute; the Unknowable; the Causeless Cause

correspondences.label: Comparisons in the text
correspondences.value: Parabrahmam; Nuit; Tao; Spinoza’s Substance; the Egyptian image of threefold darkness

correspondences.label: Symbol
correspondences.value: Ananta, the serpent enclosing the universe with its tail in its mouth

sections.title: Before form and naming
paragraphs: The opening quotation from the Zohar imagines a condition before any form has been produced. The author then explains why the intellect cannot describe it directly: a thing can be named through its distinctions, while Ain provides no distinction for a name to grasp.

He brings together Rabbi Azariel’s account of the limits of language and Blavatsky’s description of a boundless, eternal principle. The aim is to approach an origin beyond ordinary thought and perception.

sections.title: Images of the limitless
paragraphs: Nuit expresses absolute space through the star-filled night sky. The Tao comparison approaches a reality beyond the alternatives of speech and silence, existence and non-existence. Spinoza’s Substance contributes the idea of something whose conception depends on no other thing.

The serpent Ananta, surrounding the universe and taking its own tail into its mouth, expresses infinity returning into itself. These are the author’s analogies for the same problem of representing what has no boundary.

sections.title: Ain, Ain Soph and Ain Soph Aur
paragraphs: At the beginning of the Kether entry, the account moves from Ain to Ain Soph, Infinity, and then to Ain Soph Aur, Absolute Limitless Light. Through contraction, that light is described as concentrating into the primordial point of Kether.
The three veils remain above the numbered Tree. They give successive ways of contemplating its origin; Kether is the first sephirah in the manifested sequence.

veils.title: Ain Soph
veils.subtitle: Infinity · Limitless
paragraphs: Ain Soph is Infinity, or the Limitless. In the chapter’s sequence it follows Ain and precedes Ain Soph Aur, the Absolute Limitless Light.
The book uses this sequence to approach the origin of manifestation: the infinite is expressed through Kether, and the other sephiroth unfold from that first point until the sequence reaches Malkuth.

source.title: Israel Regardie · A Garden of Pomegranates

correspondences.label: Sequence
correspondences.value: Ain → Ain Soph → Ain Soph Aur → Kether

correspondences.label: Relation to the Tree
correspondences.value: The infinite approached through Kether and the emanation of the ten sephiroth

correspondences.label: Relation to Malkuth
correspondences.value: Shechinah as the spiritual presence of Ain Soph within the material world

sections.title: From infinity to manifestation
paragraphs: The brief formulation on page 43 describes Ain becoming Ain Soph and then Limitless Light in order to become comprehensible to itself. The later discussion expands the account: Ain Soph gives rise to the world through Kether and the successive sephiroth.
The chapter compares this sequence with the progression from unity to duality, trinity and multiplicity. It uses number as a way to follow the unfolding of differentiated existence.

sections.title: The limits of an explanation
paragraphs: Regardie points out the difficulty in treating an abstract zero as an agent that does something. He discusses Infinite Space, Eternal Duration and Absolute Motion as aspects through which the Absolute has been contemplated.

The Great Breath of Brahma is one of the images used: worlds appear and withdraw with a cosmic exhalation and inhalation. Another account presents manifestation as the play of Nuit and Hadit, space and its central point. The author ultimately acknowledges that the intellect cannot fully account for the first emergence.

sections.title: Presence in the Kingdom
paragraphs: In the Malkuth entry, Shechinah is described as the spiritual presence of Ain Soph abiding within material life. This connects the limitless origin with the completed Tree, and accompanies the teaching that Kether and Malkuth are present in one another in different ways.

veils.title: Ain Soph Aur
veils.subtitle: Absolute Limitless Light
paragraphs: Ain Soph Aur is Absolute Limitless Light, written Ain Soph Aour in these pages. It follows Ain and Ain Soph and is the veil immediately above Kether.
The book describes the light concentrating, through the contraction called Tsimtsum, into a central dimensionless point. That point is Kether, the Crown, from which the numbered Tree unfolds.

source.title: Israel Regardie · A Garden of Pomegranates

correspondences.label: Sequence
correspondences.value: Ain → Ain Soph → Ain Soph Aur → Kether

correspondences.label: Process described
correspondences.value: Tsimtsum — contraction or concentration into the primordial point

sections.title: Light and the first point
paragraphs: The passage uses light to express the transition from the limitless to the beginning of distinct manifestation. Kether is described as a point without dimension, the first definite principle in the Tree and the root of what follows.
An alternative image on the same page describes whirling forces heralding the primordial point. Both formulations lead from the unbounded origin to Kether’s unity.

sections.title: The author’s comparisons
paragraphs: Regardie relates this Limitless Light to Daivaprakriti in the Vedantic comparison he gives, and to Adi-Buddha or Amitabha in his Buddhist comparison. These are analogies within the book’s comparative method.
Ain Soph Aur remains part of the account preceding the ten sephiroth. The Aces, white, diamond and other correspondences that follow in the chapter belong to Kether itself.
